text: Case Study 14

name: TextBox 2
text: Race Condition in XV6 Shared Data

name: TextBox 3
text:
Demonstrating Data Inconsistency & Spinlock Synchronization
in the XV6 Kernel Free-List Allocator

name: TextBox 4
text: Platform: XV6 RISC-V  •  QEMU (2 CPUs)  •  WSL Ubuntu

name: Rectangle 1
text: 1. Problem Statement

name: Rectangle 3
text: Multiple CPUs in XV6 share kernel data structures like the physical memory free list.

name: Rectangle 4
text: Without synchronization, concurrent access causes race conditions.

name: Rectangle 5
text: Two CPUs can read the same free-list head and return the same page to different processes.

name: Rectangle 6
text: This leads to duplicate page ownership — corrupting memory.

name: Rectangle 7
text: Goal: Demonstrate the inconsistency, then fix it using XV6's spinlock.

name: Rectangle 1
text: 2. Introduction — Objectives

name: Rectangle 3
text: Understand race conditions and critical sections in kernel code.

name: Rectangle 4
text: Identify shared kernel data structures (kmem.freelist) in XV6.

name: Rectangle 5
text: Study why mutual exclusion is required for multi-CPU access.

name: Rectangle 6
text: Demonstrate data inconsistency when the lock is absent.

name: Rectangle 7
text: Show how XV6's spinlock prevents inconsistent results.

name: Rectangle 8
text: Based on Case Study 14: Race Condition in XV6 Shared Data.

name: Rectangle 1
text: 2. Introduction — Motivation

name: Rectangle 3
text: Modern CPUs have multiple cores — kernel code runs in true parallelism.

name: Rectangle 4
text: A single corrupted page allocation can crash the entire OS.

name: Rectangle 5
text: Understanding synchronization is essential for OS and systems programming.

name: Rectangle 6
text: XV6 is a small, real OS — ideal for studying these mechanisms.

name: Rectangle 7
text: XV6 runs on QEMU with configurable CPU count, making it perfect for multi-core experiments.

name: Rectangle 1
text: 3. Existing System — Background

name: Rectangle 3
text: XV6 manages free physical memory as a linked list (kmem.freelist).

name: Rectangle 4
text: kalloc() pops the head page; kfree() pushes a freed page back.

name: Rectangle 5
text: A spinlock (kmem.lock) protects all accesses to the free list.

name: TextBox 6
text: Table 1. Shared kernel structures and their locks

name: Rectangle 8
text: Source: MIT xv6 RISC-V kernel source code.

name: Rectangle 1
text: 3. Existing System — Drawbacks

name: Rectangle 3
text: Single global lock → CPUs spin-wait under high contention.

name: Rectangle 4
text: If the lock is removed, no mechanism prevents concurrent modification.

name: Rectangle 5
text: The production allocator cannot be safely tested without risking kernel crash.

name: Rectangle 6
text: No built-in diagnostic to detect or report race conditions.

name: Rectangle 7
text: These drawbacks motivate a safe, isolated test module for experimentation.

name: Rectangle 1
text: 4. Proposed Solution

name: Rectangle 3
text: Test-only kernel module mirrors the free-list pattern on two QEMU CPUs (harts).

name: Rectangle 4
text:
XV6 production allocator
kept intact and safe

name: Rectangle 5
text:
racecheck.c
Miniature list: P0 → P1 → P2

name: Rectangle 6
text:
CASE 1 · UNLOCKED
Both CPUs pop without a lock
Inconsistent ownership

name: Rectangle 7
text:
CASE 2 · SPINLOCK
acquire()/release() protect the pop
Consistent ownership

name: Rectangle 1
text: 5. Working Flow — The Critical Section

name: Rectangle 3
text: The kalloc() function performs a two-step operation on shared data:

name: Rectangle 4
text:
acquire(&kmem.lock);           // Step 1: Acquire the lock
r = kmem.freelist;             // Step 2: Read the head pointer
if (r)
    kmem.freelist = r->next;   // Step 3: Advance the head
release(&kmem.lock);           // Step 4: Release the lock

name: Rectangle 5
text:
1 · ACQUIRE
acquire(&kmem.lock)

name: Rectangle 6
text: Step 2 (read) and Step 3 (update) depend on each other.

name: Rectangle 7
text: If another CPU changes the head between those steps, Step 3 uses a stale value and the assumption breaks.

name: Rectangle 8
text: Source: kernel/kalloc.c — XV6 production allocator.

name: Critical-section step 2
text:
2 · READ
r = kmem.freelist

name: Critical-section step 3
text:
3 · UPDATE
kmem.freelist = r->next

name: Critical-section step 4
text:
4 · RELEASE
release(&kmem.lock)

text: 6. Implementation — Spinlock Path (Fix)

name: Rectangle 3
text: XV6's acquire()/release() wraps the entire critical section:

name: Rectangle 4
Rectangle 5
text: First CPU gets P0, second waits → then gets P1. No duplicates.

  same page returned twice: NO

  page IDs appearing exactly once: 3 / 3
  invariant: CONSISTENT

text: 8. Conclusion — What We Learnt

name: Rectangle 3
text: A lock must cover the full read-and-update that preserves an invariant.

name: Rectangle 4
text: Without mutual exclusion, two CPUs return the same page — data corruption.

name: Rectangle 5
text: XV6's spinlock (acquire/release) serializes access to the critical section.

name: Rectangle 6
text: The same principle applies to any shared structure: process tables, buffers, caches.

name: Rectangle 7
text: Key learning: synchronization is not optional in multi-CPU kernels.

name: Rectangle 1
text: 8. Conclusion — Future Scope & Applications

name: Rectangle 3
text: Test with more CPUs (4, 8) to study increased contention.

name: Rectangle 4
text: Implement per-CPU free lists to reduce lock contention.

name: Rectangle 5
text: Explore other primitives: mutex, semaphore, reader-writer locks.

name: Rectangle 6
text: Apply to real-world systems: database engines, web servers, RTOS.
